newsitem.title: USA: Steady policy shows Fed will wait to see inflation.
newsitem.headline: Steady policy shows Fed will wait to see inflation.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady shows that the central bank will respond to inflation when it sees it, not when it is a mere blip on the horizon -- and an arguable one at that, analysts said.

The Fed's decision to hold interest rates steady mildly surprised the Treasury market, where many worried that recent gains in hourly wages and a low unemployment rate were harbingers of impending inflation. The Fed, by declining to raise rates, seemed to respond with a traditional Midwest expression of skepticism -- "I'm from Missouri; show me."

"You haven't seen signs of inflation in the core PPI (Producer Price Index) or the core CPI (Consumer Price Index) up until this point and that probably played an integral role in the decision," said Kevin Flanagan, first vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said he was "a little surprised that the Fed did not perceive that it had to tighten."
Since Platt expects second-half economic growth to slow to below 2.0 percent, he did not think the Fed needed to tighten.

But Platt said the Fed's decision to leave rates unchanged shows that Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and the Federal Reserve Board "clearly, clearly are actually waiting to see inflation. They're not going to make bets based on wage inflation. They're not going to be pre-emptive like they were in 1994," he said.
And Platt said the next wave of U.S. economic statistics would add credibility to the Fed's steady rate policy.

"People should be bullish on the fixed-income outlook and the bullishness should be confirmed in the wave of weak data that is coming up," he said. Platt cited expected weakness in the August durable goods orders report, due on Thursday. He said he expects August new home sales, due Monday, to be down 4.0 percent. The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) September index due next Tuesday should be near 51.5 and "then on Friday (October 4), the employment report should be up only 140,000 on (non-farm) payroll employment," he said.
Economist Neal Soss, senior advisor to CS First Boston Corp, said the Fed made the correct decision.
"The Federal Reserve has told us that they are not allergic to growth," said Soss. "They are, of course, allergic to and ever-watchful for inflation -- but not to growth."
Soss said so far, the evidence shows that growth continues while inflation remains invisible.

"When the patient's blood pressure is under control, you don't change the medication," said Soss. "The Fed has plenty of time to consider when inflation will materialize and in what magnitude," he said.

In the latest Reuter poll, 31 of 55 economists surveyed said they expected the Fed to raise interest rates at the September 24 Federal Open Market Committee policy meeting. Most of those said the central bank would raise official rates by 25 basis points and that the decision to do so would be a close one.
